index.description: Fell asleep on the bus and missed your stop? Shuttles with no announcements, subway stop alarms underground, silent alerts in the library — practical ways to never miss your stop.
index.heading: How to never miss your stop
index.lead: Tricks you can use right now, with or without an app — and how to get woken up by location instead of time.

bus-stop-alarm.title: Fell asleep on the bus and missed your stop? Here’s how to stop it happening
bus-stop-alarm.description: Dozed off on the bus and woke up past your stop? Why time alarms, announcements and map apps fall short, and how to set up a location-based bus stop alarm that wakes you on arrival.
bus-stop-alarm.keywords: bus stop alarm, wake me up at my stop, fell asleep on the bus, missed my stop, bus arrival alert, stop alarm app
bus-stop-alarm.summary: Why time alarms, announcements and map apps fall short — and how to use a location alarm.
intro: A warm bus on the way home, you close your eyes for a second — and the view outside is suddenly unfamiliar. You’re two or three stops past yours, waiting for a bus back.
It happens to everyone on a tired day. Rather than fighting sleep, it’s more reliable to have **something that wakes you up**.

sections.heading: What you can try without an app
paragraphs: Each of these works to a degree, with clear trade-offs.
items: **A time alarm** — set it for your usual travel time. Simple, but traffic or a late bus makes it ring too early or too late, and a ringing phone isn’t great on a quiet bus.
**Announcements and stop displays** — fine when you’re awake, easy to miss when you’re asleep or listening to music.
**Map app navigation** — shows where you are, but only if you keep checking the screen. Useless once you doze off.

sections.heading: Why location beats time
paragraphs: The same bus route takes a different amount of time every day. So the reliable trigger isn’t ‘in 25 minutes’ but **‘when I get near my stop’**.
A location alarm draws a circle around your stop and alerts you the moment you enter it. Traffic jams and early arrivals don’t change where your stop is.

app.heading: Setting it up in EarLocAlert
paragraphs: You only set it up once. After that, you never need to open the app.
items: Pin your stop on the map and save it as an **arrival alert**.

Choose the radius while you see the circle. Buses move fast, so give yourself **a little extra distance** to get ready to get off — smaller in the city where stops are close together, larger on express routes.
Set the vibration to **Strong** so you feel it even in a pocket.
With earphones in, you also hear the alert through them. Without earphones it only vibrates — **it never uses the speaker.**
Only riding on weekday evenings? Set days and hours so it stays quiet on weekends.

faq: There’s no single right answer. Think about how fast the bus travels between stops and how long you need to get ready, start generous and shrink it after a ride or two. You can choose anything from 50 m to 2 km.
Do I need to keep the app open?
No. Once a place is saved, it watches in the background and alerts you even with the app closed and the screen off.

shuttle-bus-stop-alert.title: How to get a stop alert on a shuttle bus with no announcements
shuttle-bus-stop-alert.description: Work shuttles and campus shuttles rarely have named stops or announcements, and transit apps don’t know their routes. Here’s how to never miss your shuttle drop-off.
shuttle-bus-stop-alert.keywords: shuttle bus stop alert, work shuttle alarm, company shuttle, campus shuttle stop, shuttle drop-off reminder, employee shuttle
shuttle-bus-stop-alert.summary: Get an alert at your drop-off even when the shuttle has no stop names or announcements.
intro: Falling asleep on the work shuttle is the most natural thing in the world — early morning, a quiet bus, the same road every day. The catch: **shuttles don’t announce stops.**
Many stops have no name at all, and transit apps don’t carry the route. You’re left recognising your stop from the view out the window.

sections.heading: What you can try without an app
items: **Ask a colleague** — reliable, but awkward to ask every day.
**Remember a landmark** — a building or junction just before your stop. Doesn’t help once you’re asleep.
**A time alarm** — shuttles leave on schedule, so it works better than on a city bus, until traffic gets in the way.

sections.heading: Shuttles need something that doesn’t rely on stop data
paragraphs: Most bus and subway arrival alerts need the route and stop data to work. Shuttles don’t have that data, so those features can’t help.
A location alarm works from **a point you pin yourself** on the map. The office gate, your dorm, the airport drop-off — unnamed places work just as well.

app.heading: Setting it up in EarLocAlert
items: Pin **the exact spot where you get off** — the office gate or the front of your dorm.
Pick a radius so it wakes you a little before the shuttle stops. You choose while seeing the circle.
Set days and hours so it rings **only on weekday mornings** and stays quiet at weekends.
Several drop-offs? Save each one separately and switch them on or off individually.

faq: Does it work for shuttles that aren’t in any transit app?
Yes. It doesn’t use route data at all — only the point you pinned on the map. Unnamed stops are fine.
Do I have to turn it on and off every day?
No. Set days and hours once and it only alerts during that time.

subway-station-alarm.title: Subway stop alarm: does it work underground?
subway-station-alarm.description: Dozed off on the subway and missed your station? An honest look at why location alerts can be slower deep underground, and how to choose a radius so you still get off at the right stop.
subway-station-alarm.keywords: subway stop alarm, metro station alarm, wake me up at my station, missed my subway stop, underground GPS, train stop alert
subway-station-alarm.summary: Why location can lag underground, and how to set a radius so you don’t miss your station.
intro: The subway is even easier to fall asleep on than a bus — steady motion, nothing to see outside. There are announcements, but music in your earphones drowns them out.
So does a location alarm work underground? Honestly: **it depends on the section of track.**

sections.heading: Why location can lag underground
paragraphs: Phones estimate location from GPS, Wi-Fi and cell signals. Deep underground those signals are weaker, so **location can update later or be less precise.** On above-ground sections and near stations it’s usually fine.
That’s why on the subway the key is a **generous radius**, not one drawn tightly around the station.

sections.heading: What you can try without an app
items: **Listen for announcements** — keep your music low enough to hear them.
**A time alarm** — trains are fairly punctual, so this works better than on buses, but delays throw it off and a ringing phone draws looks.

app.heading: Setting it up in EarLocAlert
items: Pin your station and choose **a radius that allows for the distance between stations**. Waking a stop early just gives you time to get ready.
Worried about a deep section? **Also save the station before yours.** Two alerts are better than none.
With earphones in, the alert sound plays through them, so you hear it even if you miss the announcement. Without earphones, it only vibrates.

faq: Does it not work underground at all?
It does work, but deep underground the phone may find your location later, so the alert can come later. A generous radius or also saving the previous station makes a miss much less likely.
No. Arrival is detected on your phone, and your places and history stay on the device.

silent-alarm-library.title: Silent alerts for libraries and offices: vibration and earphones only
silent-alarm-library.description: Ever had an alarm blast from the speaker in a library or meeting? How to get alerts with vibration and earphones only, and how to stop alarms leaking from the speaker even when earphones are in.
silent-alarm-library.keywords: silent alarm, vibration alarm, earphone only alarm, library alarm, alarm without speaker, quiet alert app
silent-alarm-library.summary: Alerts by vibration and earphones only — never leaking from the speaker.
intro: The moment an alarm goes off through the speaker in a quiet library, every head turns. Surprisingly often it happens even when you had earphones in.
That’s because, depending on the phone and the app, **alarm sounds can play through the speaker even with earphones connected.**

sections.heading: What you can try without an app
items: **Silent mode + a vibration alarm** — blocks sound, but it’s based on time, so it can’t tell you when you arrive somewhere or leave.
**Smartwatch vibration** — a quiet tap on the wrist. Set phone notifications to mirror to your watch.

sections.heading: The point is to never use the speaker
paragraphs: In a quiet place you don’t need a quieter sound — you need **a guarantee that nothing comes out of the speaker**. One leak is one too many.

EarLocAlert checks connected devices against an **allow list**. It only plays sound through wired, USB-C or Bluetooth earphones; if it can’t confirm them, it only vibrates. Devices that play out loud, like car audio, aren’t on the list.

app.heading: Using it in quiet places
items: You can also get an alert **when you leave** the library or office — save it as a departure alert if there’s something to remember on the way out.
Choose Light, Medium or Strong vibration to suit where you are.
Mirror phone notifications to a Galaxy Watch or Apple Watch to feel alerts on your wrist.

faq: If earphones can’t be confirmed at the moment of the alert, it only vibrates. It never switches to the speaker.
Yes. It includes ads, but never on the screen that is alerting you.
